questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical skills in diagnosing listen backlog vs FD limits under bursty load using only built‑in tools, plus safe mitigation with observability.

## Key Concepts
- Listen backlog and somaxconn; accept queue pressure during bursts
- ss for socket/process mapping; Recv-Q as a pressure signal
- RLIMIT_NOFILE and per‑process fd limits; safe global and service‑level tweaks
- Safe mitigations vs disruption; confirm after changes

## Code Example
```bash
# Locate the listening socket and owner
ss -ltnp | awk '$1=="LISTEN"{print $0}'

# Read current backlog settings
cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_max_syn_backlog

# Apply safe mitigations
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=4096

# Inspect FD limits for the listener process
PID=$(ss -ltnp | awk '/LISTEN/ && /:443/ {split($NF,a,"pid="); print a[2]}')
cat /proc/$PID/limits

# Reload service and observe
nginx -s reload || systemctl reload nginx
ss -ltnp | grep LISTEN
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate observability after applying changes without full restart?
- If Recv-Q remains high, what next steps would you take to isolate the root cause?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to diagnose power/perf interplay in production Linux stacks, a common source of tail latency. By focusing on CPU frequency scaling, turbo behavior, and per-core observability, candidates demonstrate practical debugging fluency under real workloads.

- CPU frequency scaling and turbo behavior
- Per-core visibility via /sys and /proc
- isolcpus, cpuset, and sched_setaffinity for pinning
- Observability during bursts and correlating with workload

## Code Example

```bash
# Per-core governor and freq state
for cpu in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor; do echo -n "$cpu => "; cat "$cpu"; done
for freq in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq; do echo -n "$freq => "; cat "$freq"; done

# Turbo detection

# Mitigation (pinning + freq fix)
echo performance | tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor

# Pin critical threads (example)
taskset -c 0-3 <pid_of_service>
```

- How would you validate latency improvement after changes?
- What if some cores don’t reach the fixed freq due to power/bios policies?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests real-world ability to diagnose kernel allocator issues under high-concurrency, multi-tenant load using only default Linux tools—a common but often under-specified root cause of tail latency spikes. ## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to diagnose scheduler-related tail latency and apply confinement with cpusets and cgroups, without adding new tools. It emphasizes observability during targeted mitigations.

## Key Concepts
- CFS scheduling and CPU throttling via cpuset and cpu.max
- /proc/sched_debug and /sys/fs/cgroup interfaces
- pidstat/mpstat for per-process and per-CPU visibility
- Safe mitigations: pinning, adjusting quotas/weights

## Code Example
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
PID=$(pgrep -f 'critical-service')
echo PID=$PID
top -b -n1 -H | grep -w $PID
pidstat -p $PID 1
mpstat -P ALL 1
if [ -e /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.max ]; then echo 'cpu.max:'; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.max; fi
# Mitigations
taskset -cp 0-3 $PID
if [ -e /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.max ]; then echo 'Setting cpu.max to 100000 100000'; echo '100000 100000' > /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.max; fi
```

- What metrics would you collect long-term to validate stabilization?
